title: On stories in teaching
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino reflects on how stories and hinterland fit into explicit instruction, prompted by a drawing video tutorial that spent too long on shark facts. She describes her own shift from fun-and-engaging, differentiated, guide-on-the-side lessons toward explicit instruction with a visualiser, and argues that stories about figures such as Rosalind Franklin or Semmelweis genuinely draw students in. Her caution is that stories can swallow the lesson, so that students attend to the anecdote while the core content becomes an afterthought. Her remedy is to plan the hinterland as carefully as the core, so that narrative frames and supports the key message instead of drifting into tangents.
points: Explicit instruction does not have to be boring; well-chosen stories can enthral a class and link back to the content being learned.
Stories that run longer than the core teaching risk making engagement the goal instead of knowledge transfer.
Hinterland should be planned as deliberately as the core so it frames the key message rather than producing tangents.
The author's own early focus on being graded Outstanding, learning styles and differentiation is offered as what she now sees as mistaken planning.
quotes: Explicit instruction has been a game changer for the way I teach. During my early teaching years, too much of my time was taken up by thinking about how to make my lessons fun and engaging so I could be graded Outstanding (I never was).

In recent years, I have been using a visualiser and a book to draw out simple diagrams and model how to answer questions. Most of my planning involves the actual learning of the content and the questions I will ask.
Hinterland, however, supports the core and draws my students in through the stories I tell.

There needs to be a fine balance between delivery of the core and narration of the hinterland, that supports and frames the former. A way to ensure this is the case is to plan the hinterland just as well as the core.

There is a place for unplanned stories, personal feelings and experiences when teaching. But having a good idea of how to frame the core content with relevant stories and historical events makes the overall delivery efficient rather than rambling. It serves to focus attention on the key message rather than going off on irrelevant tangents.
Otherwise we risk focusing on engaging our students over transferring knowledge- a thought that sends shivers down my spine.
